gloss_terse: Gachar or Gahar, head of a family of returned exiles mentioned in Ezra and Nehemiah
gloss_readable: Gachar (also spelled Gahar) appears as the head of a family of temple servants who returned from Babylonian exile. The name occurs in parallel lists of returnees in both Ezra and Nehemiah, confirming this family's place among the repatriated community that helped rebuild Jerusalem's worship life.

senses.1: A personal name designating the patriarch of one of the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned with Zerubbabel from exile. The dual attestation in Ezra 2:47 and Nehemiah 7:49 reflects the careful record-keeping of post-exilic community organization, with the family identified as 'sons of Gachar' in both genealogical registers.

gloss_terse: rejoicing, exultation; a verbal noun expressing jubilant celebration
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes rejoicing or exultation, capturing the emotional intensity of celebration. Isaiah uses it twice in contexts of eschatological joy—once in the oracle promising the wilderness will blossom with 'joy and singing' (35:2), and again in the vision of Jerusalem recreated as 'a rejoicing' (65:18). The word's rarity underscores its poetic and prophetic register.

senses.1: An abstract noun of action denoting jubilant rejoicing or exultation. In Isaiah 35:2, it appears in construct with 'and singing,' describing the wilderness transformed into a place of celebration. In Isaiah 65:18, God promises to create Jerusalem as 'a rejoicing' itself—not merely a place where people rejoice, but rejoicing personified. The multilingual evidence (Spanish 'con gozo,' English 'with joy') confirms the celebratory, joyful character of this term.

gloss_terse: the Gilonite, a gentile adjective referring to an inhabitant of Giloh
gloss_readable: This gentile designation identifies someone from the town of Giloh in the hill country of Judah. Most famously, Ahithophel the Gilonite served as David's counselor before defecting to Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 15:12). The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 11:36 preserves the same designation, though with a textual variant in the Hebrew manuscript tradition.

senses.1: A gentile adjective meaning 'of or from Giloh,' used to identify Ahithophel's hometown origin. The term appears in 2 Samuel 15:12 during the account of Absalom's conspiracy, and in 2 Samuel 23:34 among David's mighty men (with a parallel in 1 Chronicles 11:36). The definite article typically accompanies the term in Hebrew, reflecting standard gentile usage ('the Gilonite').

gloss_terse: Ginath, the father of Tibni who contended for Israel's throne after Omri
gloss_readable: Ginath appears only as the father of Tibni, who challenged Omri for kingship over Israel following Zimri's death. The brief civil war ended with Tibni's defeat and Omri's establishment of a new dynasty. Though Ginath himself plays no active role in the narrative, his name is preserved in both references to his son's failed bid for power.

senses.1: A personal name identifying the father of Tibni, who led a faction opposing Omri's claim to the throne of Israel. Both occurrences in 1 Kings 16:21-22 appear in the phrase 'Tibni son of Ginath,' serving to distinguish this royal contender by his patronymic. The name's Semitic root may relate to 'garden,' though its precise etymology remains uncertain.

gloss_terse: Giloh, a town in the hill country of Judah, home of Ahithophel
gloss_readable: Giloh was a town in the mountainous region of Judah, assigned to that tribe in the territorial allotments of Joshua. It gained historical significance as the hometown of Ahithophel, David's counselor who later joined Absalom's rebellion. The town's name may derive from a root meaning 'to uncover' or 'to reveal,' though the connection remains uncertain.

senses.1: A place name designating a town in the hill country of Judah. Joshua 15:51 lists it among the settlements in Judah's inheritance, while 2 Samuel 15:12 identifies it as Ahithophel's hometown ('from Giloh'). The multilingual glosses consistently render it as a proper name (Spanish 'Guiló,' French 'Giloh'), and the prepositions in Hebrew (מן 'from,' conjunction 'and') show it functioning as a standard geographical designation.

gloss_terse: tablet, mirror; possibly polished metal surfaces or fine gauze garments
gloss_readable: This rare noun appears in two distinct contexts with possible meanings. In Isaiah 8:1, God instructs the prophet to 'take a large tablet' for writing a prophetic inscription. In Isaiah 3:23, it occurs in a list of luxury items worn by wealthy women, interpreted either as polished metal mirrors or as translucent, gauze-like garments. Ancient versions diverged on the meaning, reflecting genuine interpretive uncertainty.

senses.1: A term denoting either a writing surface or a reflective/transparent object. As a tablet (Isaiah 8:1), it serves as a medium for public prophetic inscription, described as 'large' (gadol). In the context of feminine adornment (Isaiah 3:23), it may refer to polished metal mirrors (so Targum and Vulgate) or fine, see-through fabrics (so Septuagint). The Hebrew root may relate to revealing or uncovering, which could support either interpretation depending on context.

gloss_terse: folding, turning; describing hinged door leaves
gloss_readable: This adjective describes the folding or turning mechanism of door leaves in Solomon's temple. The term appears twice in the description of the inner sanctuary's cypress doors, each with two leaves that could fold or turn. The word captures the architectural innovation of hinged, bi-folding doors in the temple's construction.

senses.1: An adjective meaning 'folding' or 'turning,' used to describe the movable leaves (panels) of doors. Both occurrences in 1 Kings 6:34 refer to the same architectural feature: 'two leaves of the one door were folding, and two leaves of the other door were folding.' The root relates to rolling or revolving motion, suggesting doors that could pivot or fold back upon themselves, rather than swinging on simple hinges.

gloss_terse: cylinder, rod; cylindrical supports or ornamental posts
gloss_readable: This noun denotes cylindrical objects, appearing in two poetic contexts. In Esther 1:6, it describes silver rods or posts supporting the rich hangings of Ahasuerus's palace courtyard. In Song of Songs 5:14, it's used metaphorically of the beloved's hands, likened to 'cylinders of gold set with topaz'—possibly referring to fingers adorned with rings or the cylindrical form of the hands themselves.

senses.1: A noun meaning cylinder, rod, or cylindrical post. The term appears in construct forms describing ornamental or structural elements. In Esther 1:6, 'rods of silver' (alongside marble pillars) support expensive fabrics in a royal setting. In Song 5:14, 'cylinders of gold filled with topaz' provides a luxurious simile for the beloved's hands, suggesting either finger rings on cylindrical fingers or hands shaped like decorated rods. The root relates to rolling or circular motion, emphasizing the round, tubular shape.

gloss_terse: Gallim, a place north of Jerusalem, home of Palti and mentioned in Isaiah's oracle
gloss_readable: Gallim (meaning 'heaps') was a town located north of Jerusalem, somewhere along the invasion route described in Isaiah's oracle against Assyria. It appears as the hometown of Palti, to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal after David fled. Isaiah personifies the town as 'daughter of Gallim,' urging her to cry out as the enemy approaches.

senses.1: A place name designating a town in Benjamin's territory north of Jerusalem. First Samuel 25:44 identifies it as Palti's hometown (Michal was given to 'Palti from Gallim'), while Isaiah 10:30 includes it in the prophetic invasion route approaching Jerusalem, with the city personified as 'daughter of Gallim' called to raise her voice in alarm. The name means 'heaps' or 'ruins,' possibly referring to topographical features.

gloss_terse: rolling, great; describing large, rolled stones too heavy to carry
gloss_readable: This noun describes stones characterized by their rolling quality—massive stones that had to be rolled rather than carried. Both biblical occurrences appear in Aramaic sections of Ezra, describing the construction of the Second Temple with 'stones of rolling' or 'great stones.' The term emphasizes the stones' size and the method required to move them.

senses.1: A noun meaning 'rolling' used attributively to describe large building stones. In Ezra 5:8 and 6:4, the phrase 'stones of rolling' (eben gelal) refers to massive hewn stones used in temple construction, so heavy they could only be moved by rolling them into place. The term derives from the root גלל meaning 'to roll,' and the multilingual evidence ('great,' 'grande') captures the implication of size that necessitates rolling rather than lifting.

gloss_terse: Galeed, the name Jacob gave to the witness-heap covenant with Laban
gloss_readable: Galeed (meaning 'witness-heap') is the name Jacob gave to the pile of stones erected as a covenant witness between himself and Laban. While Laban called it by the Aramaic equivalent Jegar-sahadutha, Jacob used this Hebrew name. The site marked both a covenant boundary and a memorial, later associated with the region of Gilead.

senses.1: A place name meaning 'heap of witness' or 'witness-pile,' given by Jacob to commemorate his covenant with Laban at the stone cairn they erected together. Genesis 31:47-48 records both the Aramaic name (Jegar-sahadutha, used by Laban) and the Hebrew name (Galeed, used by Jacob) for the same location. The name combines 'gal' (heap) and 'ed' (witness), and the biblical narrative explicitly connects it etymologically to the later name Gilead.

gloss_terse: descend, sit; possibly describing flocks moving down a mountainside
gloss_readable: This rare verb appears only in Song of Songs, used twice in identical poetic imagery comparing a woman's hair to 'flocks of goats that descend from Mount Gilead.' The verb's precise meaning remains uncertain—it may mean descend, sit up, or recline. The construction and sense are somewhat awkward, leading to various interpretive proposals.

senses.1: A verb of uncertain meaning, possibly 'descend' or 'sit/recline,' used in a simile comparing hair to goats on a mountainside. Both occurrences (Song 4:1, 6:5) appear in the identical phrase 'that descend/sit from Mount Gilead,' describing the visual effect of dark goats moving down a terraced hillside, their undulating motion evoking flowing hair. The root may be related to Arabic 'sit up,' though 'descend' fits the context more naturally. The multilingual glosses favor 'descend' (Spanish 'descienden,' French 'descendent').

gloss_terse: swallow, drink, devour; taking in liquids or consuming eagerly
gloss_readable: This verb denotes swallowing or drinking, appearing in two quite different contexts. In Genesis 24, Abraham's servant asks Rebekah to let him 'sip' or 'drink' a little water. In Job 39, the same root describes a warhorse that 'swallows' the ground in its furious gallop—a vivid metaphor for speed and eagerness. The verb captures both literal drinking and figurative consuming.

senses.1: A verb meaning to swallow, sip, or drink in liquid. In the Hiphil stem (Genesis 24:17), it means 'cause to drink' or 'let drink'—the servant asks Rebekah to 'let me sip a little water.' In the Piel stem (Job 39:24), it intensifies to 'swallow' or 'devour,' used metaphorically of a horse that 'swallows the ground' in its charging gallop. The multilingual evidence captures both the gentle drinking (Spanish 'sorber,' German 'schlürfen') and the vigorous consuming (Spanish 'devora').

gloss_terse: theft, stolen thing; property taken unlawfully
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes something stolen or the act of theft itself. It appears in Exodus 22 within the legal code governing property crimes. The law addresses both the stolen item itself and the circumstances of the theft, including whether the thief is caught in the act or afterward. The term is concrete, referring to specific stolen property rather than theft as an abstract concept.

senses.1: A noun meaning 'stolen thing' or 'theft,' referring to property unlawfully taken. In Exodus 22:3 (English 22:4), it designates the actual stolen animal that must be restored. In Exodus 22:2 (English 22:3), it appears in the phrase 'for his theft' (literally 'in his theft'), describing the legal status of a thief caught in the act. The construct form (genevah) and the form with suffix (bigenevato) both point to concrete stolen goods rather than the abstract concept of stealing.

gloss_terse: Genubath, son of Hadad the Edomite and an Egyptian princess
gloss_readable: Genubath was the son of Hadad the Edomite (Solomon's adversary) and the sister of Queen Tahpenes of Egypt. Raised in Pharaoh's household alongside Egyptian princes, Genubath represents the intermarriage between Edomite royalty and Egyptian nobility. His name appears twice in the brief account, emphasizing his unique position bridging two royal courts.

senses.1: A personal name identifying the son born to Hadad and the Egyptian queen's sister. Both occurrences in 1 Kings 11:20 appear in the same verse, first naming him at birth and then describing how he was weaned and raised in Pharaoh's palace among the royal children. The name may be related to the root for 'steal' or 'theft,' though the significance of such an etymology remains unclear. The final tav (ת) represents an archaic or dialectal form of the name.

gloss_terse: low, bellow; the sound cattle make
gloss_readable: This verb describes the lowing or bellowing of cattle, capturing the distinctive sound oxen make. Job uses it rhetorically, asking whether an ox lows over its fodder when satisfied. In 1 Samuel, the Philistine lords hear the cows 'lowing as they went' while pulling the ark back to Israel—a detail highlighting the animals' reluctance to leave their calves behind.

senses.1: A verb meaning to low, bellow, or make the characteristic sound of cattle. In Job 6:5, it appears in a rhetorical question: 'Does the ox low over its fodder?' (implying: of course not, when satisfied). In 1 Samuel 6:12, it describes the sound of cows walking: 'going along the road and lowing' as they pulled the cart bearing the ark. The term is onomatopoetic, mimicking the sound itself, and appears across languages with similar translations (Spanish 'muger,' German 'brüllen').

gloss_terse: crush, gnaw, break; pulverizing bones or pottery
gloss_readable: This denominative verb means to break or crush bones, appearing in two violent contexts. Balaam's oracle describes Israel crushing the bones of their enemies. Ezekiel's oracle against Oholibah uses the same verb, though applied to gnawing pottery shards—a gesture of desperation or self-harm. Both instances emphasize thorough, violent destruction.

senses.1: A Piel verb meaning to crush, break, or gnaw bones. Numbers 24:8 uses it in Balaam's oracle: 'he shall crush their bones,' describing Israel's military dominance over enemies. Ezekiel 23:34 employs it more obscurely: 'you shall gnaw its shards,' referring to the cup of judgment drunk to the dregs. The root relates to 'bone' (gerem), making this a denominative verb specifically focused on bone-crushing action. The multilingual glosses capture both the crushing force and the gnawing action.

gloss_terse: crush, grind; be crushed or pulverized
gloss_readable: This verb denotes being crushed or grinding something to pieces. The psalmist uses it to describe his soul 'crushed with longing' for God's judgments—a powerful metaphor for intense spiritual desire. In Lamentations, Jeremiah laments that God 'has ground my teeth with gravel,' a vivid image of humiliation and bitter suffering from divine discipline.

senses.1: A verb meaning to be crushed, ground down, or pulverized. In the Qal stem (Psalm 119:20), the verb is reflexive or passive: 'My soul is crushed with longing,' using physical grinding as a metaphor for consuming desire that wears down the inner being. In the Hiphil causative (Lamentations 3:16), God is the agent: 'He has ground my teeth with gravel,' depicting humiliation through forced consumption of grit. Both uses involve the idea of crushing or grinding, whether emotional or physical, with the Aramaic cognate suggesting perishing or being destroyed.

gloss_terse: groats, crushed grain; grain kernels coarsely ground or crushed
gloss_readable: This noun refers to groats—grain that has been crushed or coarsely ground but not finely milled into flour. It appears in Leviticus' instructions for grain offerings, specifying that fresh ears of grain should be 'parched with fire, crushed grain of fresh ears.' The term emphasizes the intermediate state between whole kernels and fine flour, suitable for certain offerings.

senses.1: A concrete noun meaning groats, grits, or crushed grain—specifically grain kernels that have been crushed or ground but remain coarser than flour. Leviticus 2:14 prescribes offering 'young ears parched with fire, crushed grain of fresh fruit' as a firstfruits grain offering. Leviticus 2:16 refers back to this 'crushed grain' when specifying what the priest shall burn. The term derives from the root meaning 'to crush' and appears in cognate languages (Aramaic, Syriac) with similar meanings. Spanish and German glosses emphasize the 'crushed' or 'ground' character of this grain preparation.

gloss_terse: grope, feel; searching by touch in darkness or blindness
gloss_readable: This verb describes groping or feeling with the hands, typically when unable to see clearly. Isaiah uses it twice in one verse, painting a vivid picture of spiritual blindness: Israel gropes like the blind at noon, feeling along walls as in deep darkness. The repetition intensifies the image of helpless searching and disorientation.

senses.1: A Piel verb meaning to grope, feel, or search by touch. Both occurrences appear in Isaiah 59:10: 'We grope like the blind along a wall; we grope like those without eyes.' The repetition emphasizes the extent of spiritual darkness and moral confusion afflicting the people. The verb suggests deliberate tactile searching when sight fails, similar to cognates in Arabic, Aramaic, and Ethiopic that mean to touch, stroke, or feel. The cohortative form ('let us grope') may express either description of current reality or ironic self-exhortation.

gloss_terse: Gath-hepher or Gittah-hepher, hometown of the prophet Jonah in Zebulun's territory
gloss_readable: Gath-hepher (also called Gittah-hepher) was a town in Zebulun's tribal allotment, famous as the hometown of the prophet Jonah. The name means 'winepress of digging' or 'winepress of the well.' Located in the Galilee region, it was identified in the nineteenth century with El-Meshhed, about three miles northeast of Nazareth.

senses.1: A place name meaning 'winepress of the pit/well,' designating a town in Zebulun. Joshua 19:13 lists it in the boundary description as 'Gittah-hepher,' while 2 Kings 14:25 identifies it as 'Gath-hepher,' the home of 'Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet.' The slight variation in spelling (Gittah vs. Gath) represents the same location. The multilingual evidence shows consistent treatment as a proper geographical name with various transliterations.

gloss_terse: Gittaim, a town in Benjamin where Beerothites fled as refugees
gloss_readable: Gittaim was a town in the territory of Benjamin, serving as a refuge for people from Beeroth who fled there and remained as resident aliens. The name suggests a dual form, possibly meaning 'two winepresses' or 'twin presses.' The site's exact location remains unknown, though it lay somewhere in Benjamin's hill country.

senses.1: A place name in Benjamin, appearing in two forms: 'Gittaim' (Nehemiah 11:33) in a list of Benjaminite settlements, and 'to Gittaim' with directional suffix (2 Samuel 4:3) describing where the Beerothites fled and became resident aliens. The dual ending (-ayim) in the name suggests paired features, possibly two winepresses or a double settlement. The spelling variation (Gittayim/Gittaim) represents dialectal or scribal differences for the same location.

gloss_terse: Gether, a son of Aram listed in the Table of Nations
gloss_readable: Gether appears in the genealogical Table of Nations as one of Aram's sons, making him a grandson of Shem and part of the Semitic line. The name occurs in both Genesis and Chronicles in the parallel genealogies tracing post-flood peoples. His descendants presumably formed an Aramean tribe or people group, though no further biblical information identifies them.

senses.1: A personal name identifying one of the four sons of Aram in the Table of Nations. Genesis 10:23 and its parallel 1 Chronicles 1:17 both list Gether among Aram's descendants, placing him in the Semitic family tree. The name's etymology is uncertain. The consistent preservation of the name in both genealogical accounts suggests historical memory of an Aramean clan or people group, though no other biblical texts identify Gether's descendants.

gloss_terse: pasture, pastureland; grazing land for flocks
gloss_readable: This noun denotes pasture or grazing land where flocks feed. It appears in two prophetic contexts—Isaiah's oracle of judgment reversed and Micah's promise of restoration. Both passages use the image of sheep feeding in their proper pasture to symbolize peace, security, and divine provision for God's people returned from judgment.

senses.1: A noun meaning pasture or pastureland. Isaiah 5:17 depicts lambs feeding 'as in their pasture' (or 'according to their pasture'), suggesting normal, peaceful grazing after desolation. Micah 2:12 uses a similar image: 'like a flock in the midst of its pasture,' depicting restoration and abundance. The Aramaic cognates (dabra, Syriac dabro) confirm the pastoral meaning. The term appears with possessive suffixes, emphasizing belonging—the pasture proper to each flock.

gloss_terse: cause, reason, purpose; the intent or grounds for something
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun means cause, reason, or purpose, appearing in the book of Daniel in prepositional phrases. It introduces the purpose or explanation for an action, similar to 'in order that' or 'because.' Daniel uses it to explain why the mystery was revealed and why the decree about the tree was given.

senses.1: An Aramaic noun meaning 'cause' or 'reason,' used in construct phrases to express purpose or intent. Daniel 2:30 states the mystery was revealed 'for the purpose that the interpretation might be made known,' while Daniel 4:17 (Aramaic 4:14) explains the decree is given 'to the intent that the living may know' God's sovereignty. The phrase 'al-dibrath di' functions as a compound preposition meaning 'for the purpose that' or 'to the intent that.' The Biblical Hebrew cognate (דָּבָר) shares this sense of 'matter, cause, affair.'

gloss_terse: gather, brood, hatch; collecting together as a bird with young
gloss_readable: This verb describes gathering or brooding like a bird with its young. Isaiah uses it of the arrow-snake (or perhaps kite) gathering in its shadow to nest and hatch. Jeremiah employs it metaphorically of a partridge that 'gathers eggs it did not lay,' illustrating ill-gotten wealth that won't last. Both passages evoke the image of a bird collecting and incubating.

senses.1: A verb meaning to gather together, brood, or hatch, with the semantic range of a bird collecting its young or eggs. In Isaiah 34:15, the arrow-snake (or kite) 'gathers' or 'nests' in the ruins of Edom, with the verb suggesting brooding or hatching in the shadow. In Jeremiah 17:11, the partridge 'gathers but does not hatch'—or 'broods over eggs not laid'—serving as a metaphor for acquiring wealth unjustly. The Aramaic cognate means 'heap together,' supporting the gathering sense. The verb captures both the physical collecting and the incubating care of brooding birds.

gloss_terse: walk slowly, move deliberately; walking in procession or with measured pace
gloss_readable: This verb denotes slow, deliberate movement—walking at an easy pace or moving in solemn procession. The psalmist recalls leading the festival procession slowly and deliberately to the house of God. Hezekiah, after his illness, laments that he must 'walk softly' or carefully all his years because of his affliction. The verb suggests measured, intentional movement rather than rushed haste.

senses.1: A verb meaning to move slowly, walk deliberately, or proceed at a measured pace. In Psalm 42:4, the Piel stem may mean 'lead slowly' in procession (though MT has Hithpael 'walk slowly'), describing the solemn movement of worshipers to the temple. In Isaiah 38:15, the Hithpael means 'I will walk softly' or 'go carefully'—Hezekiah's response to affliction, suggesting cautious, deliberate living. The New Hebrew and Aramaic cognates support the sense of leading or walking slowly, possibly in ceremonial contexts. The root contrasts with rapid movement, emphasizing controlled, intentional pacing.

gloss_terse: Dodanim or Rodanim, descendants of Javan, possibly referring to Rhodians or people of Rhodes
gloss_readable: This gentile plural designates descendants of Javan (Greeks) in the Table of Nations, likely referring to inhabitants of Rhodes or the surrounding islands. Genesis reads 'Dodanim' while the parallel 1 Chronicles text has 'Rodanim,' with most scholars preferring the latter as original (reflected in Septuagint's 'Rhodians'). The confusion between Hebrew letters dalet and resh explains the variant.

senses.1: A gentile plural name identifying a people group descended from Javan (Ionian Greeks) in the Table of Nations. Genesis 10:4 has 'Dodanim' while 1 Chronicles 1:7 reads 'Rodanim,' with the latter likely original—referring to Rhodes or Rhodians, as supported by the Septuagint rendering. The names are graphically similar in Hebrew (ד/ר confusion), explaining the textual variation. These descendants represent one of the Aegean or Mediterranean island peoples in the Japhetic genealogy.

gloss_terse: galloping, dashing; the sound or action of horses charging at full speed
gloss_readable: This feminine plural noun captures the galloping or dashing of horses, specifically cavalry charges. It appears only in Deborah's song, where the repetition 'galloping, galloping' intensifies the image of pounding hoofbeats as enemy horsemen flee in panic. The doubling creates an onomatopoetic effect, echoing the rhythmic thunder of horses at full gallop.

senses.1: A noun (plural construct) meaning gallopings, dashings, or charges, specifically referring to the pounding movement of horses at full speed. Judges 5:22 uses intensive repetition: 'from the galloping, galloping of his steeds'—the doubled noun creates a drumbeat effect mimicking the sound of hoofbeats. The term derives from a root meaning 'rush' or 'dash,' and the context is Sisera's fleeing cavalry. The multilingual evidence ('galopar,' 'galloping') consistently captures the rapid, rhythmic motion of charging horses.

gloss_terse: fishermen, fishers; those who catch fish for livelihood
gloss_readable: This plural noun designates fishermen or those engaged in fishing. Isaiah's oracle against Egypt laments that 'the fishermen will mourn' when the Nile fails. Jeremiah's judgment oracle declares God will send for 'many fishermen' to catch the people of Judah. Ezekiel envisions fishermen standing along the shores of the healed Dead Sea. The term consistently refers to the occupation of fishing.

senses.1: A masculine plural noun meaning fishermen or fishers—those who fish for a living. The term appears with variant spellings: Isaiah 19:8 and Ezekiel 47:10 have 'dayagim' (Qere), while Jeremiah 16:16 shows both Ketiv ('davagim' or 'dawagim') and Qere ('dayagim') forms. All refer to professional fishermen affected by or participating in divine judgment and restoration scenarios. The root relates to 'fish' (dag), making this a clear occupational designation. Translations consistently render it as 'fishermen' or 'fishers.'

gloss_terse: illness, languishing, sickness; the state of being sick or weakened by disease
gloss_readable: This noun denotes illness, sickness, or languishing—the state of being physically weakened or diseased. The psalmist speaks of God sustaining him on his 'bed of illness.' Job uses it metaphorically, comparing his sufferings to disease in his food—something loathsome and repulsive. The term emphasizes the debilitating, weakening aspect of sickness.

senses.1: A noun meaning illness, sickness, or languishing condition. Psalm 41:3 (English 41:4) uses it in construct: 'bed of languishing/illness,' describing physical sickness that confines one to bed. Job 6:7 employs it more obscurely: 'they are like disease in my food' (or 'loathsome as my food'), using illness as a metaphor for repulsive suffering. The term derives from a root suggesting weakness or faintness, and emphasizes the debilitating nature of disease rather than specific symptoms. The Syriac cognate confirms the sense of sickness or weakness.

gloss_terse: hoopoe, a crested bird listed among unclean birds in Levitical law
gloss_readable: This noun designates the hoopoe, a distinctive crested bird with a long curved beak, listed among unclean birds in the dietary laws. The hoopoe (Upupa epops) is native to the Middle East and known for its striking crown of feathers. Both Leviticus and Deuteronomy include it in the catalog of birds Israelites were forbidden to eat.

senses.1: A feminine noun identifying the hoopoe, a specific bird species classified as ritually unclean. Leviticus 11:19 and Deuteronomy 14:18 both list it among prohibited birds, typically appearing with the definite article ('the hoopoe'). The bird is likely Upupa epops, recognized by ancient versions (Septuagint, Vulgate, Saadia) as the hoopoe. Some scholars suggest the name may be of Egyptian origin. The hoopoe's distinctive appearance and habits made it easily identifiable in the ancient world, and it remains common in Israel today.

gloss_terse: silence, the realm of the dead; the stillness of Sheol
gloss_readable: This feminine noun means silence, specifically the silence of death or the grave. The psalmist contrasts the living who praise God with the dead who 'go down to silence.' Another psalm warns that without God's help, he would dwell 'in silence'—a poetic term for Sheol. The word evokes the eternal stillness of the grave, where no voice rises in praise.

senses.1: A noun meaning silence, used as a poetic designation for Sheol or the realm of the dead. Psalm 94:17 states 'my soul would soon dwell in silence,' using silence as a synonym for death or Sheol. Psalm 115:17 declares 'the dead do not praise the LORD, nor any who go down to silence,' contrasting living worshipers with silent corpses. The term emphasizes the cessation of speech, praise, and all vocal activity in death. Some scholars also see it in Isaiah 21:11 ('oracle of silence'), though that may refer to Dumah as a place name.

gloss_terse: circle, ball; a round shape or circular formation
gloss_readable: This noun denotes something circular or round—either a circle or a ball. Isaiah uses it metaphorically when God threatens to whirl someone away 'like a ball' into a distant land—an image of judgment and exile. The term also appears in a disputed text where God camps 'in a circle' around Jerusalem, though textual variants and interpretations differ. The basic sense involves roundness or circular shape.

senses.1: A noun meaning circle, ball, or round object. In Isaiah 22:18, God will 'whirl you around and around and throw you like a ball into a wide land'—a vivid image of being cast away in judgment. Isaiah 29:3 is textually uncertain, possibly meaning 'I will camp in a circle around you' (though some read 'like David'). Ezekiel 24:5 may use it for 'pile' or 'heap' (of bones under a pot), though this is disputed. The root suggests circular motion or shape, and Talmudic usage confirms the meaning 'ball.'

gloss_terse: stumbling, being pushed down; the state or danger of falling
gloss_readable: This noun denotes stumbling or being pushed down, appearing in two nearly identical psalms. The psalmist praises God for delivering his feet 'from stumbling'—preventing his fall into death or destruction. The term captures both the physical danger of tripping and the spiritual or mortal peril it represents.

senses.1: A noun meaning stumbling or the state of being pushed/thrust down. Psalm 56:13 and 116:8 contain identical phrases: 'You have delivered... my feet from stumbling,' thanking God for preventing the psalmist from falling (whether literally or into death/disaster). The term derives from a root meaning 'thrust' or 'push,' suggesting being forcibly knocked down rather than merely losing one's footing. The preposition 'from' (min) indicates rescue or prevention from this fate.

gloss_terse: thrust, crowd, oppress; pushing forcefully or crushing by pressure
gloss_readable: This verb means to thrust, crowd, or press together, often with hostile intent. Joel describes the disciplined advance of locusts who don't 'jostle' each other despite their vast numbers. The book of Judges uses it of enemies who 'maltreated and oppressed' Israel, combining physical and social violence. The verb conveys forceful pushing or crushing pressure.

senses.1: A verb meaning to thrust, crowd, press, or oppress. Joel 2:8 describes locusts in formation: 'they do not jostle one another,' emphasizing their orderly advance despite crowding. Judges 2:18 uses a participial form: 'their oppressors and those who crushed them,' referring to enemies who physically and politically pressed Israel. The root appears in Aramaic with similar meanings (to press, crowd, oppress), and the Arabic cognate means 'drive away' or 'remove.' The verb emphasizes forceful pressing or hostile crowding.

gloss_terse: fishermen, fishers; those who catch fish (Qere reading)
gloss_readable: This is the Qere (standard reading) form for fishermen, appearing in texts where the written Ketiv has slight orthographic variations. The term designates professional fishermen, whether mourning the Nile's failure in Egypt or standing along the shores of the restored Dead Sea in Ezekiel's vision. The Qere/Ketiv variants reflect dialect or spelling differences without changing the meaning.

senses.1: The Qere form of the masculine plural noun meaning fishermen or fishers. Isaiah 19:8 and Jeremiah 16:16 both show this as the preferred reading (with Ketiv variants), while Ezekiel 47:10 uses it as well. In Isaiah, the fishermen mourn Egypt's disaster; in Ezekiel, they stand along the healed Dead Sea ready to fish in newly living waters. The term is occupational, referring to those who fish for livelihood, whether with nets, hooks, or other methods.

gloss_terse: kite, vulture; a bird of prey listed among unclean birds
gloss_readable: This feminine noun designates a bird of prey, likely the kite or a type of vulture, listed among unclean birds in Levitical law. The bird is associated with desolate, ruined places—Isaiah's oracle describes it nesting in the ruins of Edom. Both dietary law passages classify it as unfit for consumption, grouping it with other raptors and scavengers.

senses.1: A noun identifying a specific unclean bird, probably the kite (genus Milvus) or a related vulture. Deuteronomy 14:13 lists 'the kite' (with definite article) among prohibited birds, while Isaiah 34:15 uses the plural form, depicting these birds nesting and hatching in Edom's ruins—behavior consistent with raptors that frequent desolate areas. The bird's habitat preference for ruins and its classification with other birds of prey support identification as a kite or small vulture. Ancient versions vary in their specific identifications.

gloss_terse: Dimon, an alternate name for Dibon in Moab, used in Isaiah's oracle
gloss_readable: Dimon is an alternate name for Dibon, a major Moabite city north of the Arnon River, appearing only in Isaiah's oracle against Moab. Isaiah uses 'Dimon' instead of the usual 'Dibon,' possibly for wordplay with 'dam' (blood), since the waters of Dimon are filled with blood. The city is the same as biblical Dibon, modern Dhiban, famous for the Moabite Stone discovery.

senses.1: A variant place name for Dibon (which appears elsewhere in Scripture), used twice in Isaiah 15:9: 'the waters of Dimon are full of blood' and 'I will bring more upon Dimon.' The spelling variation from Dibon to Dimon may be intentional, creating wordplay with 'dam' (blood), since the oracle emphasizes Moab's bloodshed. The reference to 'waters of Dimon' likely indicates the Arnon River near the city. This is the same Moabite city mentioned extensively elsewhere as Dibon.

gloss_terse: judge, administer justice (Aramaic); exercising judicial authority
gloss_readable: This Aramaic verb means to judge or exercise judicial authority. It appears in Ezra when Artaxerxes authorizes Ezra to appoint magistrates and judges who will 'judge' all the people in the Trans-Euphrates region who know God's law. The term designates official legal adjudication, parallel to the Hebrew verb for judging.

senses.1: An Aramaic Peal participle meaning 'judges' or 'those who judge.' Ezra 7:25 appears twice (Ketiv and Qere variants) with the meaning 'judges who judge the people.' The Ketiv reads 'da'anin' while the Qere has 'dayanin,' both from the root meaning 'to judge.' The context is appointing officials to administer justice according to God's law. The participle functions as a noun designating judicial officers or magistrates, equivalent to Biblical Hebrew 'shophetim.'
